evals.prompt: We run Parcelform, a shipping-label API for e-commerce backends. A pentest just flagged that the 40-character random API keys we issue to merchants sit in plaintext in a Postgres 'keys' table. My tech lead wants to fix it exactly like our user passwords: bcrypt at cost 12, then on each request loop over the account's key rows and bcrypt-compare until one matches. Before we build that, spec the storage schema and the request-path lookup flow for us.
evals.expected_output: A storage design that rejects the bcrypt plan for machine-generated keys: SHA-256 hash-only storage with an indexed plaintext prefix column for lookup, constant-time comparison, structural pre-validation, async last-used telemetry, and lifecycle columns supporting rotation.
expectations: Recommends SHA-256 (fast hash) over bcrypt for the stored key hashes
Grounds the choice in entropy: slow hashes exist to defend low-entropy human passwords, and brute force is infeasible against a high-entropy generated key at any per-hash cost
Cites bcrypt's 72-byte input truncation as a mechanical strike against bcrypt for long keys
Points out that salted slow hashes cannot be looked up by hash equality, breaking the proposed loop-and-compare design
Adds a short indexed plaintext key_prefix column for O(1) candidate lookup
Requires constant-time comparison on the final hash check, naming the timing leak of a naive equality comparison
Schema carries lifecycle columns: owner, scopes, created_at, last_used_at, expires_at or equivalents
Lookup flow begins with structural validation (known prefix, length, checksum) rejecting malformed keys before any database round-trip
Writes last_used_at asynchronously, fire-and-forget, never blocking the request path on telemetry
Scopes default restrictive; omitted scopes never mean full access
States the entropy-floor precondition (at least ~120 bits / 32+ random characters) that makes fast hashing safe
Keeps the default rung irretrievable: full key shown exactly once at creation, only the hash stored afterward
Treats zero plaintext keys at rest as the gate, verified by schema audit rather than policy assertion
Designs storage to support two simultaneously valid keys per identity (expires_at doubling as the rotation grace window, no unique-active-key constraint)

evals.prompt: I'm the platform PM at Nimbusgrid, a serverless hosting provider. Our v1 API keys are bare UUIDv4 strings. Last month a customer committed one to a public GitHub repo and it sat exploitable for three weeks before their own auditor caught it. We're designing the v2 token format now. One engineer argues UUIDs already have 122 bits of randomness so the format is fine and we just need to email customers about hygiene. What should v2 keys look like, and what do we do about leaks like that one?
evals.expected_output: A v2 key format of prefix + high-entropy body + checksum built for scanner detectability, with environment encoded in the prefix, Secret Scanning Partner Program registration justified by the real incident, and immediate revocation of the leaked key.
expectations: Rejects bare UUID keys on detectability grounds (indistinguishable from other encoded data, unscannable by secret scanners), not merely on entropy
Specifies the prefix + high-entropy random body + checksum structure for v2 keys
Prefix encodes key type and environment
Encodes test vs live environment in the prefix from day one
Sets an entropy floor of at least 120 bits (32+ random characters)
Cites the GitHub-style benchmark: roughly 30-character Base62 body around 178 bits plus a CRC32 checksum
Explains the checksum's double duty: a validator rejects malformed keys without a database round-trip, and scanners filter noise before alerting
Accepts roughly 10 characters of extra token length as an overhead explicitly worth paying
Recommends registering the v2 pattern with GitHub's Secret Scanning Partner Program, justified by the real leaked-key incident
Describes the partner mechanics: an HTTPS endpoint receives reported matches, and any reported match is treated as compromised - revoke and notify the owner
Rejects customer-hygiene emails as the control: structural detectability replaces user vigilance
Treats the already-leaked key as confirmed compromise requiring immediate zero-grace revocation
Notes partner-pattern alerts run automatically on public repositories, enabling revocation before the customer notices the leak

evals.prompt: Ledgerhawk here - we sell an accounting API to about 4,000 tenants. Enterprise prospects keep failing us on security review because we have no key rotation story. Current plan from ops: generate fresh keys for every tenant in one batch, email them out on the 1st, and disable every old key the following Monday. They also want a standing rule that all keys rotate every 30 days, because that's what auditors like. Design our rotation.
evals.expected_output: A zero-downtime rotation design replacing the mass cutover: per-key atomic roll with dual-key overlap, telemetry-gated deletion, staged cutover, scenario-based grace windows, and pushback on the fixed 30-day cadence.
expectations: Rejects the one-shot mass cutover: rotation is per-key dual-key overlap where old and new keys validate simultaneously for a grace period
Exposes rotation as a single atomic roll operation that creates the new key and schedules the old key's expiry in one call
Warns against splitting rotation into two manual steps where the expiry half gets forgotten
Recommends a routine grace window in the 24-hour-to-7-day range, tied to deploy cadence
Reserves zero-grace immediate revocation for compromise or offboarding, never routine rotation
Gives agent fleets and queued workloads a longer grace window than the human default
Requires last-used telemetry and forbids disabling or deleting an old key before its traffic hits zero
Sequences deactivate-then-delete with a 24-48 hour wait, noting deactivation is reversible and deletion is not
Cites a named vendor dual-key mechanic (Stripe's up-to-7-day roll or AWS's two-active-key cap forcing overlap)
Pushes back on the universal 30-day rule: no universal rotation frequency exists, cadence must be justified against risk profile and deploy cadence
Fires an expiry-approaching alert and extends the window when old-key traffic persists, rather than breaking a live consumer
Stages the cutover: staging first, then production, then agent fleets and queued workloads last
Logs every rotation step (initiator, timing, grace window chosen) as audit evidence
States the doubled-attack-surface invariant: never create a new key without scheduling the old one's revocation

evals.prompt: Our senior platform engineer at Corvid Metrics resigned yesterday, effective immediately. We've discovered the Salesforce sync, the billing cron, and two customer-facing integrations all authenticate with API keys he created under his personal account. My boss's take: the keys still work, nothing is broken, we'll clean it up next quarter. Also there's no screen anywhere that shows which keys he created or could see. What's the right move?
evals.expected_output: An immediate offboarding response: enumerate and zero-grace revoke the leaver's keys, rotate shared credentials, reissue the integrations on service-account keys, log everything, and install the ownership model and admin visibility that prevent a recurrence.
expectations: Rejects waiting until next quarter: a departed employee's still-valid personal keys are treated as a live incident
First step enumerates every key the leaver created or could see, flagging the missing admin key-inventory view as a gap to build
Revokes the leaver's user-owned keys with zero grace, explicitly accepting the downtime
Rotates shared or org credentials the leaver had access to, not only their personal keys
Reissues the four integrations on service-account or org-owned keys, never on another employee's personal keys
Defines the service-account property: credential validity decoupled from any human's employment status
Labels production integrations running on personal keys a standing process failure, not a one-off cleanup
Logs every offboarding action for the audit trail and access-review evidence
Recommends a permanent org-admin filterable view of every key a given user created or can see
Sets the forward ownership policy: individual keys reserved for personal experimentation, production and automation on service accounts or org keys
Adds org-tier governance: admin approval before issuance and admin review and revocation of members' keys
Installs an offboarding runbook to run on every future departure
Requires every live key to carry an owner, scope documentation, and an expiry or documented exemption going forward

evals.prompt: Fintar processes card payments through our API. Two things landed on me this week. Our new compliance hire insists PCI requires rotating every API key every 90 days and wants budget for a rotation tool. And sales promised a big enterprise deal contingent on SOC 2 Type II, audit scheduled in 10 weeks, so the plan is to write our key-management policy the week before the auditor shows up. Sanity-check both.
evals.expected_output: Corrects the PCI 90-day myth with the actual Requirement 8.6.3 obligations (risk-analysis-justified cadence, unconditional compromise rotation), and flags the SOC 2 Type II plan as failing by construction given the observation-window requirement, with evidence automation as the fix.
expectations: Corrects the myth: PCI-DSS 4.0 does not mandate any fixed rotation interval
Names Requirement 8.6.3 (or the 8.6.x set) and notes it became mandatory in 2025
Requires the cadence to be justified by a documented targeted risk analysis (Requirement 12.3.1), which the auditor will ask to see
States compromise-triggered rotation is unconditional - immediate on suspicion or confirmation, regardless of the analyzed cadence
Links complexity to cadence: slower rotation demands stronger keys, satisfied by a high entropy floor
Covers the PCI logging obligation: tamper-resistant logs retained 12 months with the latest 3 months immediately accessible
Flags the SOC 2 plan as failing by construction: Type II requires controls operating consistently across a 3-12-month observation window
Distinguishes Type I (point-in-time) from Type II, noting a week-before policy could at most satisfy Type I
States SOC 2 auditors check evidence the policy operates (key-event logs, periodic access reviews, approval records), not that it exists
Names the relevant criteria (CC7.2 / C1.2) or the required lifecycle coverage: provisioning, rotation, revocation, destruction
Recommends automating evidence generation from day one rather than assembling it before the audit
Maps auditor expectations to product features: mandatory expiration, expiry warnings and forced-rotation reminders, audit logging of every key event, service accounts
Requires documenting the rationale for the chosen authentication mechanism, since 'it was already there' is itself an audit finding

evals.prompt: I run platform at Traceloom, a monitoring SaaS. Three items: (1) partners want to build apps that read our customers' dashboards on those customers' behalf - my plan is to extend our API keys with per-request scopes, short expiry, and per-app revocation so we don't need a whole new auth system; (2) the new browser SDK must call our ingest API straight from the customer's frontend, so we'll document pasting the API key into the JS snippet; (3) each customer's CI pipeline runs on a single long-lived admin key we issued, stored in their runners. Review all three.
evals.expected_output: A boundary review: plan (1) is reinventing OAuth and hands off to authorization-server design, plan (2) is rejected in favor of server-minted ephemeral tokens, and plan (3) moves toward workload identity federation with interim scoping of the admin keys.
expectations: Names plan (1) as reinventing OAuth: bolting expiry, per-request scopes, and fine-grained revocation onto static keys means adopting the real thing
Routes third-party apps acting on customers' behalf to OAuth authorization-server design instead of solving it inside the key system
States the boundary: a static key answers which app is calling, OAuth answers whether a user granted permission and within what limits
Invokes the principle that an API key identifies the calling application, not a user, and is not user authentication
Rejects plan (2) outright: never ship a long-lived key to a browser or other semi-trusted client
Substitutes server-side minting of short-lived scoped tokens (ephemeral, minutes-long TTL) for the browser SDK
For CI, recommends workload identity federation - the environment attests, so no stored secret exists to leak
States workload identity's trade honestly: highest effort (federation infrastructure) bought for nothing-to-leak security
Contains the current admin keys in the interim: scope them down and split per service per environment, with rotation scheduled
Frames the choice per surface, not per platform: mature platforms run keys and OAuth simultaneously
Keeps first-party server-to-server traffic on static keys rather than migrating every surface to OAuth
Identifies CI and agent workloads as the segment actively migrating off static keys

evals.prompt: Voltmesh sells an energy-metering API. Today every customer gets exactly one key that can do everything on the account: meter reads, tariff writes, billing changes, user management. A big customer asked for read-only keys. Our PM's proposal: keep it simple - new keys stay full-access by default, and customers who care can untick permissions in an advanced panel at creation. Worth noting we already run a mature 40-permission RBAC system for our web app. What scoping model should we ship?
evals.expected_output: A scoping design that rejects both the account-wide key and the fail-open default, ships per-environment split plus restrictive-by-default coarse scopes, and re-ranks fine-grained scoping as nearly free given the existing RBAC.
expectations: Rejects the single account-wide do-everything key outright as the anti-pattern, not an acceptable bottom rung
Rejects the fail-open default: keys must be restrictive by default, and an opt-out unticking panel is the named failure to design against
Names or describes the SendGrid precedent (omitted scopes at creation granting full access) as the fail-open example
Sets the expansion rule: widen a key's scope only when usage logs prove the consumer needs more
Recommends both bottom rungs together: one key per service per environment plus a coarse read/write per-product-area scope set
States the stacking payoff: a leaked key then compromises one service in one environment with one permission set
Re-ranks the ladder against the existing RBAC: reusing the 40-permission system makes fine-grained scoping nearly free, flipping the effort ordering and the winner
Describes the fine-grained rung concretely: per-resource grants, granular permissions, mandatory expiration
Positions scoping as authorization layered on the identity the key establishes - complementary controls, not substitutes
States that team or internal-service trust is not a security boundary; the key's own scope is the only enforceable one
Requires documenting every key by what it does: name, consuming service, allowed and denied actions, owning team
Pairs scoping with expiry, citing the undocumented never-expiring key that becomes invisible infrastructure
Separates billing and administrative permissions from ordinary read/write scopes so one key never holds both

evals.prompt: Quillhook is a newsletter-sending API used mostly by hobbyist developers. Support burns hours every week on 'I lost my API key' tickets. Engineering's proposal: store keys AES-encrypted with a key kept in the app's config file so the dashboard can re-display them anytime, and make the API fall back to a built-in default key when the env var is missing so local dev never breaks. Right now the dashboard also prints the full key on every page load, which we figured is fine once we can re-show keys anyway. Redesign key storage and the dashboard.
evals.expected_output: A retrievable-rung design done right: AES-256-GCM with a KMS-held key-encryption-key, SHA-256 hash for request-path validation, audit-logged explicit reveal, masked list views, no fallback key, and the full self-service action set.
expectations: Accepts the retrievable rung as legitimate for this profile (low-stakes data, lost-key support load dominates) rather than forcing hash-only storage
Replaces app-config encryption with AES-256-GCM whose key-encryption-key is held in a KMS, never application-managed
Stores a SHA-256 hash alongside the ciphertext so request-path validation never performs a decrypt
Restricts decryption to an explicit dashboard reveal action that is itself audit-logged
Names the compliance cost of going retrievable: it creates a surface an auditor samples (KMS key custody plus the reveal path)
Rejects the built-in fallback key: a missing secret must crash the service at startup, because a hardcoded dev fallback authenticates in production exactly like a real key
Masks keys everywhere after creation (first and last characters only), removing the full-key-on-every-page-load display
Specifies the list view per key: human-readable label, creation date, last-used timestamp, status badge, and direct rotate/revoke actions
Verifies all four self-service actions complete without a support ticket: sign up, create a key, rotate a key, revoke a key
Updates last-used asynchronously, fire-and-forget, off the request path
Presents the alternative honestly: on the hash-only rung the lost-key path is reissue, so retrievability is a deliberate trade, not the default
Separates per-key usage (and spend) from the last-used signal: one answers whether the key is alive, the other what it is doing
